segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Good afternoon, everyone!

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This is the first seminar in preparation for our archaeological fieldwork in Namibia; we are fantastically lucky to have received partial research funding for this trip from our Institute, so I shall expect 200% attention and participation from you all.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: First in this seminar, I'm going to give a brief introduction to contemporary research on rock art, and in the second part I'm going to give you some do's and don'ts for our fieldwork trip in April - so please listen very carefully.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: I'm first going to focus on the interpretation of rock art in Namibia.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: We are very fortunate to be going to an area where you can find some of the most important sites in the entire world.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And I hope to show you how easy it is for everyone to make mistakes in looking at cultures which are different from our own - the first and most important lesson we have to learn.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In Namibia there are both paintings and engravings - that's where the surface of the rock is cut out.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Many of the engravings show footprints of animals and most scholars used to think that the purpose of these was simple and obvious: this rock art was like a school book with pictures to teach children about tracks: which track belonged to which animal - giraffe, lion and so on.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But there were some mysteries.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: First, when you look at a typical Namibian painting or engraving, you see the tracks are repeated, there are dozens of tracks for the same animal.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: You'd expect just one clear illustration if the reason -the aim- was to teach tracking.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now there were two more problems.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Why are some of the engravings of animals very accurate as you'd expect- all clearly identifiable- and others quite unrealistic?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And another mystery - some of these unrealistic animals - that's in the engravings - seem to be half human.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Some, for , have got human faces.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Many researchers now think that these were pictures the wise men engraved of themselves.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: They believed they could use magic to control the animals they had drawn, so the hunters could then catch them for food.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This shows you some of the dangers of coming from one culture to another, as we'll be doing, without understanding it fully.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Scholars imagined that children looked at rock art pictures to learn to track- just because they themselves had learnt skills from pictures; many researchers now believe that rock art had a much more complex purpose.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And we'll talk more about it next week!

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now before I invite you to ]oin in a discussion in this second part of the seminar, I'd like to make some very important points about our fieldwork - and in fact any field trip to look at rock art.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: We're going to a number of sites, and we won't always be together.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The single largest problem faced by people who manage the sites is- yes, I'm sure you've guessed - damage caused by visitors, even though it's usually unintentional.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Whenever you do go to a site, don't forget you can learn many things from observing at a distance instead of walking all over it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This can really help to reduce visitor pressure.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: People often say, 'Well, there's only two of us and just this one time', but maybe thousands of people are saying the same thing.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And then some basic rules to guide you -we'll have our own camp near a village, but remember never to camp on a site if you go on your own.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It may be disrespectful to the people of that culture, and certainly don't make fires, however romantic it may seem.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It's really dangerous in dry areas, and you can easily burn priceless undiscovered material by doing so.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So, how are we going to enjoy the rock art on our field trip?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: By looking at it, drawing it and photographing it- NEVER by touching it or even tracing it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Rock art is fragile and precious.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Remember that climbing on rocks and in caves can destroy in a moment what has lasted for centuries.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So no heroics in Namibia, please!

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Try to be extra careful and help others to be too.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And lastly please don't even move rocks or branches to take photographs - you should leave the site intact- I'm sure I can rely on you to do that.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Well, that's about all I want to say before today's first discussion, but if you have any questions please ask them now- and don't forget you'll find some fascinating information about world-wide sites on the Internet.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Right, first question then?
